directions.description: Bach's chorales are the gold standard of Western harmony. But what if we could MEASURE the harmonic complexity using topology? Encode each chord as a point in a 12-dimensional space (one dimension per pitch class). A sequence of chords traces a path in this space. Compute the persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a Bach chorale. Conjecture: Bach's chorales have persistent H_1 (1-dimensional cycles) that survive across a wide range of scales, indicating circular harmonic motion (the circle of fifths). In contrast, random chord sequences have H_1 bars that die quickly. The longest H_1 bar in a Bach chorale corresponds to the circle of fifths — the fundamental harmonic cycle. Pop music has shorter H_1 bars (less complex harmonic cycles). Atonal music has no persistent H_1 (no harmonic cycles). Test: compute persistent homology barcodes for 100 Bach chorales, 100 pop songs, and 100 atonal pieces. Verify: Bach has H_1 bars of length > 0.5 (in normalized pitch-class space), pop has bars of length 0.2-0.5, atonal has no persistent H_1. Impact: the topology of music IS its harmonic structure. Bach's genius is literally topological — his music has longer harmonic cycles.
directions.proof_strategy: Encode each chord as a binary vector in {0,1}^12 (pitch class set). Map to R^12 using the Fourier transform: each pitch class k maps to e^{2*pi*i*k/12}, giving a point on the unit circle. A chord maps to the sum of its pitch class vectors, normalized. Compute persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a piece using Vietoris-Rips complexes. For Bach: the circle of fifths creates a persistent H_1 cycle because chord progressions follow the circle (C -> G -> D -> A -> E -> B -> F# -> C# -> G# -> D# -> A# -> F -> C). This cycle survives across multiple scales. For pop: the cycle is shorter (typically I -> V -> vi -> IV -> I, a 4-chord loop). For atonal: no persistent cycle. Compute: Rips filtration for epsilon = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0. Measure H_1 bar lengths. Test: verify Bach H_1 bars > 0.5, pop H_1 bars 0.2-0.5, atonal H_1 bars < 0.2.
directions.title: Persistent Homology of Musical Harmony: The Topology of Bach

directions.description: The Galois group of a random polynomial over Q is S_n with probability 1. This is the Hilbert irreducibility theorem in probabilistic form. But what about random polynomials over finite fields? For f in F_p[x] of degree n chosen uniformly at random, the Galois group is S_n with probability approaching 1 as p grows. Conjecture: the probability that Gal(f) is NOT S_n is O(p^{-1/2}) for fixed n, and the exceptional cases concentrate at polynomials with discriminant zero or small Galois groups. More precisely, P(Gal(f) != S_n) = c_n / sqrt(p) + O(1/p) where c_n depends only on n. For n=2: P(Gal(f) != S_2) = P(discriminant = 0) = 1/p. For n=3: P(Gal(f) != S_3) = P(f has a rational root) = 3/p + O(1/p^2). Test: enumerate all monic polynomials of degree n over F_p for small p and n, compute Galois groups, verify P(Gal != S_n) ~ c_n / sqrt(p). Impact: random polynomials have maximal Galois groups — algebraic randomness is generic.
directions.proof_strategy: For a random monic polynomial f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 over F_p, the Galois group is a subgroup of S_n. Compute P(Gal(f) = S_n) by counting. For n=2: Gal(f) = S_2 unless discriminant = a_1^2 - 4*a_0 = 0, which happens for p choices of a_1 (each gives one a_0), so P = 1 - p/p^2 = 1 - 1/p. For n=3: Gal(f) != S_3 iff f has a rational root (3 choices of root, each determines f) or Gal = A_3 (discriminant is a square). Count both cases. For general n: use the fact that random permutations have cycle structure converging to the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. The Galois group is S_n unless there is an 'obvious' factorization, which happens with probability O(1/p). Test: implement in Lean 4 + Python. For p=2..100 and n=2..6, enumerate all monic polynomials, compute factorizations, estimate P(Gal != S_n).
directions.title: Stochastic Galois Theory: Random Permutations Have Generic Galois Groups

directions.description: Sudoku is a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Random Sudoku instances exhibit a phase transition: for n^2 x n^2 grids, the probability of having a solution drops from ~1 to ~0 around a critical density of pre-filled cells. Conjecture: the phase transition occurs at density d_c(n) = (n^2 - 1) / n^2, independent of the specific constraint structure. For standard 9x9 Sudoku (n=3): d_c = 8/9 ≈ 0.889. For 4x4 Sudoku (n=2): d_c = 3/4 = 0.75. For 16x16 (n=4): d_c = 15/16 ≈ 0.9375. The 'hardness' of random Sudoku peaks at the phase transition: instances with density near d_c take exponentially longer to solve than easy (low density) or trivial (high density) instances. Conjecture: the computational hardness of Sudoku at the phase transition is O(exp(n^2)) for backtracking algorithms, matching the theoretical prediction for CSPs at criticality. Test: generate random Sudoku instances at varying densities, measure solver time, and verify the phase transition at d_c. Impact: Sudoku hardness is not about 9x9 grids — it is about the phase transition structure of constraint satisfaction.
directions.proof_strategy: Define random Sudoku(G, d) as a G x G grid with d * G^2 cells pre-filled uniformly at random, subject to the constraint that the pre-filled cells are consistent (no two same numbers in the same row/column/box). For n^2 x n^2 grids: G = n^2. The density d = (# pre-filled) / G^2. Phase transition: P(solvable) as a function of d. For n=2 (4x4): d_c = 3/4. For n=3 (9x9): d_c = 8/9. Theoretical basis: the number of solutions of an empty G x G grid is S(G). Adding a constraint reduces the solution count by approximately S(G)/G. At density d, the number of solutions is approximately S(G) * (1 - 1/G)^{d*G^2} ≈ S(G) * exp(-d*G). This is > 0 when d < (ln S(G))/G ≈ (G-1)/G = d_c. Hardness: at density d near d_c, the expected number of backtracks is exp(O(G)). Test: generate 10000 random Sudoku instances at each density from 0.5 to 0.99, solve with backtracking, measure time, verify phase transition at d_c.
directions.title: The P vs NP of Sudoku: Phase Transitions in Constraint Satisfaction

directions.description: Anyon braiding in topological quantum computing gives unitary matrices from the braid group B_n. The Jones representation rho_k: B_n -> U((k-1)(n-1)+1) at root of unity e^{2*pi*i/k} is conjectured to be universal for quantum computation when k >= 3 and n >= 4. Conjecture: the set of all braids in B_4 under the Jones representation at k=5 generates a dense subgroup of SU(3). More precisely, the image rho_5(B_4) is an infinite subgroup of SU(3) that is not contained in any proper closed subgroup. This means that topological quantum computing with Fibonacci anyons (k=5) is universal: any unitary in SU(3) can be approximated to arbitrary precision by braiding 4 anyons. The key: the Jones representation at k=5 gives 3x3 matrices, and the braid generators sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 generate a dense subgroup of SU(3). Test: compute the Jones representation at k=5 for B_4, verify that sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 has infinite order, and check that the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 is dense in SU(3) by the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. Impact: braiding anyons is universal for quantum computation. The braid group B_4 at k=5 is a quantum gate set.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the braid group B_n = <sigma_1, ..., sigma_{n-1} | sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}>. The Jones representation at root of unity q = e^{2*pi*i/k}: for k=5, q = e^{2*pi*i/5}, the representation rho_5: B_4 -> SU(3). Compute the matrices: sigma_1 = rho_5(sigma_1), sigma_2 = rho_5(sigma_2), sigma_3 = rho_5(sigma_3). These are 3x3 unitary matrices. Verify: (1) sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, (2) sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}. Check density: compute sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 and verify it has infinite order (the trace is not a root of unity). Apply the Solovay-Kitaev theorem: if the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 contains a non-commuting pair and is infinite, then it is dense in SU(3). Test: implement in Python using numpy, compute the Jones representation matrices, verify the braid relations, and check density by approximating random SU(3) matrices.
directions.title: Topological Quantum Compiling: Braid Groups as Universal Gates

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers No form a proper class containing all real numbers, all ordinal numbers, and all infinitesimals. Every real number r has a surreal representation r = {r - 1 | r + 1}. Every ordinal alpha has a surreal representation alpha = {alpha |}. Every infinitesimal epsilon = {0 | 1, 1/2, 1/4, ...}. The surreal numbers form a field (in fact, a real-closed field). Conjecture: the subfield of surreals born by day omega (the set of surreals with finite birthdays) is isomorphic to the field of real algebraic numbers extended with all dyadic rationals. More precisely: No_{omega} = Q[2^{-n} : n in N] (the rationals extended with all dyadic rationals). The subfield born by day omega^2 contains all real numbers that are algebraic over the dyadic rationals, plus all infinitesimals that are algebraic over the reals. Conjecture: No_{omega^2} = R(x) where x is the smallest positive infinitesimal. Test: compute the field structure of surreals born by day omega and verify the isomorphism with the dyadic rationals. Impact: the surreal number hierarchy encodes the constructive hierarchy of real number fields — each birthday level adds exactly the algebraic closures needed.
directions.proof_strategy: Define No_alpha = {surreals with birthday < alpha}. No_0 = empty. No_1 = {0} = {{|}}. No_2 = {-1, 0, 1} (three surreals). No_3 = {-2, -1/2, -1, -1/4, 0, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2} (but actually No_3 has 7 surreals). By day omega: No_omega = all dyadic rationals m/2^n for m in Z, n in N. This is a field: the dyadic rationals are closed under +, -, *, / (for nonzero). Proof: m/2^n + k/2^l = (m*2^l + k*2^n)/2^{n+l} which is dyadic. Product: (m/2^n)(k/2^l) = mk/2^{n+l}. Reciprocal: 1/(m/2^n) = 2^n/m which is rational (not always dyadic). Wait: 1/3 is not dyadic. So No_omega is not closed under reciprocals of odd denominators. Correction: No_omega is the ring of dyadic rationals, not a field. The field of fractions is Q (all rationals). Conjecture revised: the field of fractions of No_omega is Q, the rationals. No_{omega^2} includes all real numbers that can be constructed by day omega^2, which includes all real algebraic numbers (since each algebraic number has a finite Dedekind cut representation). Test: enumerate surreals by birthday and verify field closure.
directions.title: The Arithmetic of Games: Surreal Numbers as Number Fields

directions.description: The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error-correcting codes are constructed from classical linear codes C_1, C_2 with C_2 perp subset C_1. The CSS code encodes dim(C_1) - dim(C_2) logical qubits. This is exactly the definition of a cohomology group: H^1(C_1, C_2) = C_1 / C_2. Conjecture: every CSS code is equivalent to a cohomology computation on a simplicial complex, and vice versa. Specifically, given a simplicial complex K, the CSS code with C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries) encodes dim(H_1(K, F_2)) logical qubits with distance d = min(length of shortest non-trivial cycle, length of shortest non-trivial cocycle). This is the homological quantum error-correcting code HQECC(K). The distance d equals the systole of K (the length of the shortest non-contractible cycle). Conjecture: for the hypercube Q_n (n-dimensional cube graph), the HQECC encodes 1 qubit with distance d = 2^{n/2} (achieving the quantum Singleton bound). Test: construct HQECC for Q_4, Q_6, Q_8 and verify the parameters. Impact: quantum error correction is cohomology. Every simplicial complex gives a quantum code, and the code parameters are topological invariants.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the CSS construction: given F_2-linear codes C_2 perp subset C_1 subset F_2^n, the CSS code is the subspace spanned by {|v + C_2> : v in C_1}. This encodes k = dim(C_1/C_2) = dim(H^1) logical qubits. Define HQECC(K): for a simplicial complex K, let C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles mod F_2) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries). Then H_1(K, F_2) = Z_1/B_1 is the first homology. The CSS code with these C_1, C_2 encodes dim(H_1) qubits. Distance: d_X = min weight of non-trivial cycle in Z_1 \ B_1, d_Z = min weight of non-trivial cocycle. The code distance d = min(d_X, d_Z). For hypercube Q_n: H_1(Q_n, F_2) = F_2^{n choose 2} (since Q_n has n choose 2 independent 1-cycles). Wait, that's for n >= 3. Actually Q_n is bipartite, so H_1 has dimension (n choose 2). The systole of Q_n is 4 (the shortest cycle). So d = min(4, something). Need to compute d_Z: the shortest non-trivial cocycle. For Q_n, d_Z = 2^{n/2} by the MacWilliams identity. Test: construct CSS codes from simplicial complexes, compute parameters [[n, k, d]].
directions.title: Quantum Error Correction from Homological Algebra: CSS Codes as Cohomology

directions.description: Sorting a list of n elements reduces the entropy from log(n!) bits to 0 bits, doing thermodynamic work W = kT * log(n!) in the process. But this is only true if sorting is irreversible — if the sorted list uniquely determines the input, then sorting is reversible and does no thermodynamic work. The key insight: comparison-based sorting makes irreversible comparisons (you learn a < b but discard the possibility a > b), and each comparison reduces entropy by at most 1 bit. So n*log(n) comparisons reduce entropy by at most n*log(n) bits, which matches log(n!) ~ n*log(n) bits. Conjecture: the minimum thermodynamic work of sorting n elements is W_min = kT * log(n!), and this work is achieved by optimal comparison-based sorting algorithms (merge sort, heapsort). Sub-optimal algorithms (bubble sort: n^2 comparisons) do more thermodynamic work than necessary: W_bubble = kT * n^2, wasting kT * (n^2 - n*log(n)) bits of entropy reduction. Conjecture: any sorting algorithm that makes C(n) comparisons does thermodynamic work proportional to C(n) * kT, and the optimal work is W_min = kT * n*log(n) (Stirling's approximation). Test: simulate sorting algorithms with entropy bookkeeping, verify W = kT * log(n!) for merge sort and W = kT * n^2 for bubble sort. Impact: sorting is a thermodynamic process. The n*log(n) lower bound is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the entropy of a permutation: S(pi) = -sum_i p_i * log(p_i) where pi is a permutation of n elements. Initially, all n! permutations are equally likely, so S_initial = log(n!) bits. After sorting, only one permutation (the identity) is possible, so S_final = 0. The thermodynamic work is W = kT * (S_initial - S_final) = kT * log(n!). Each comparison in a sorting algorithm reduces entropy by at most 1 bit: comparing a and b tells you one bit (whether a < b or a > b), reducing the number of possible permutations by a factor of at most 2. So C comparisons reduce entropy by at most C bits. For optimal sorting: C(n) = n*log(n) (merge sort), so W = kT * n*log(n) ≈ kT * log(n!) (by Stirling). For bubble sort: C(n) = n^2/2, so W = kT * n^2/2 >> kT * log(n!). The excess work is kT * (n^2/2 - n*log(n)), which is thermodynamic waste. Test: implement merge sort and bubble sort with entropy counters, verify entropy reduction per comparison.
directions.title: The Thermodynamics of Sorting: Entropy and Computational Work

directions.description: The Robertson-Seymour theorem states that the set of finite graphs is well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation: any infinite sequence of graphs contains two where one is a minor of the other. This implies that any minor-closed graph property is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. Conjecture: the same theorem holds for representable matroids over any finite field. Specifically, for any finite field F_q, the set of F_q-representable matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation. This would generalize the Robertson-Seymour theorem from graphs (F_2-representable matroids) to all finite fields. The conjecture is known to fail for general matroids (by the existence of infinite antichains of non-representable matroids), but for F_q-representable matroids with q <= 3, it is open. Conjecture: for F_3 (ternary matroids), the set of excluded minors for representability is finite. The current known excluded minors for F_3 are: the Fano matroid F_7, its dual F_7*, and the non-Pappus matroid. Test: enumerate ternary matroids of rank 3 on 9 elements, verify that all but the known excluded minors are F_3-representable. Impact: Robertson-Seymour for matroids would unify graph minor theory and matroid theory under a single well-quasi-ordering theorem.
directions.proof_strategy: Define matroid minor: M' is a minor of M if M' can be obtained from M by a sequence of deletions and contractions. The Robertson-Seymour theorem for graphs: for any infinite sequence G_1, G_2, ..., there exist i < j such that G_i is a minor of G_j. Conjecture: the same holds for F_q-representable matroids. For q=2 (graphs): this is Robertson-Seymour. For q=3: this is open. Known result: the set of excluded minors for F_3-representability is {F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus}. The conjecture would follow from: (1) F_3-representable matroids are well-quasi-ordered under the minor relation, and (2) any minor-closed class of F_3-representable matroids has finitely many excluded minors. Step (1) requires showing that F_3-representable matroids contain no infinite antichain. The known antichains (uniform matroids U_{2,n} for n >= 4) are NOT F_3-representable for large n. Step (2) follows from (1) by the same argument as Robertson-Seymour. Test: enumerate all rank-3 matroids on 9 elements (there are ~100), check F_3-representability, verify that excluded minors are exactly F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus.
directions.title: Matroid Minors and the Graph Theorem: Robertson-Seymour for Matroids

directions.description: The Collatz map T: N -> N defined by T(n) = n/2 if n even, 3n+1 if n odd, is conjectured to always reach 1. The Collatz conjecture is equivalent to: the orbit of every n under T eventually reaches the cycle {1, 4, 2, 1}. Define the Collatz Fourier transform: F_T(omega) = sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n} for N large. Conjecture: F_T has a spectral gap: |F_T(omega)| < C for all irrational omega, where C < sqrt(N). This would mean that the Collatz map does not concentrate energy at any irrational frequency — it is 'mixing' in the Fourier sense. Moreover, the spectral gap is related to the convergence rate: the wider the gap, the faster the orbit reaches 1. Conjecture: for the orbit of n, the number of steps to reach 1 is O(log(n)), which is equivalent to F_T having a spectral gap of width Omega(1/log(n)). Test: compute F_T for n up to 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with the spectral gaps of related maps (5n+1, 7n+1) which do NOT always converge. Impact: the Collatz conjecture is a spectral gap problem. Convergence to 1 means the Fourier transform has no resonances at irrational frequencies.
directions.proof_strategy: Define F_T(omega) = (1/N) * sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n}. For rational omega = p/q: F_T(p/q) measures the correlation between T(n)/n and the frequency p/q. For T(n) = n/2 (even case) or T(n) = (3n+1)/2 (odd case, accelerating), the ratio T(n)/n is either 1/2 or approximately 3/2 + 1/(2n). The spectral gap of F_T is: gap = inf_{|omega|>0} |F_T(omega)| / F_T(0). For a mixing map, F_T(omega) -> 0 as N -> infinity for irrational omega. This is the von Neumann ergodic theorem for the 3n+1 map. If the 3n+1 map is mixing (which is conjectured but not known), then F_T has a spectral gap. The connection to Collatz convergence: if T is mixing, then the orbit of n visits the set {1} with positive density, which implies it eventually reaches 1. The spectral gap width determines the convergence rate: a gap of width delta gives convergence in O(log(n)/delta) steps. Test: compute F_T(omega) for N = 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with 5n+1 (which has orbits that may diverge) and n+1 (which converges in n steps).
directions.title: The Fourier Analysis of Collatz: Spectral Gaps in the 3n+1 Map

directions.description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.
directions.proof_strategy: Given an n-player game G with strategy sets S_1, ..., S_n. Define the simplex Delta = {(p_1, ..., p_n) : p_i in Delta(S_i), sum p_i = 1}. Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.
directions.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory

directions.description: A periodic rhythm in music is a function f: Z -> {0, 1} that is periodic: f(n + p) = f(n) for some period p. The symmetry group of a rhythm with period p is a subgroup of Z/pZ. But music also has 2D patterns: a drum pattern is a function g: Z x Z -> {0, 1} (onset grid in time x pitch). The symmetry group of a drum pattern is a subgroup of Z x Z, which is a wallpaper group in 1D. In 2D, the wallpaper groups classify all possible symmetries of periodic patterns. There are exactly 17 wallpaper groups in 2D. Conjecture: the 17 wallpaper groups correspond to 17 fundamentally different types of rhythmic structure in music. Specifically: (1) p1: no symmetry (free rhythm), (2) p2: 2-fold rotational symmetry (call-and-response), (3) pm: mirror symmetry (palindrome), (4) pg: glide reflection (canon), (5) cm: mirror + glide (round), (6) pmm: double mirror (bilateral palindrome), (7) pmg: mirror + glide (inverted canon), (8) pgg: double glide (double canon), (9) cmm: double mirror + glide (round + palindrome), (10) p4: 4-fold rotation (4-bar cycle), (11) p4m: 4-fold + mirrors (variations on a theme), (12) p4g: 4-fold + glides (inverted variations), (13) p3: 3-fold rotation (3-bar blues), (14) p3m1: 3-fold + mirrors, (15) p31m: 3-fold + glides, (16) p6: 6-fold rotation (whole-tone scale symmetry), (17) p6m: 6-fold + mirrors (maximal symmetry, the 'perfect' rhythm). Test: classify 1000 drum patterns by their wallpaper group and verify the distribution matches musical practice. Impact: there are exactly 17 types of rhythm in music, classified by the wallpaper groups.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a drum pattern as a function g: Z_m x Z_n -> {0, 1} (onset grid with m time steps and n pitch classes). The symmetry group of g is the set of (a, b, R) in Z_m x Z_n x D_n such that g(R*x + a, R*y + b) = g(x, y) for all (x, y). Here D_n is the dihedral group of order 2n. For 2D patterns with translation lattice L, the symmetry group is a wallpaper group. The 17 wallpaper groups are: p1, p2, pm, pg, cm, pmm, pmg, pgg, cmm, p4, p4m, p4g, p3, p3m1, p31m, p6, p6m. Each corresponds to a different type of rhythmic symmetry. p1: no symmetry (most common in free jazz). p2: 2-fold rotation (AABB form). pm: mirror (palindromic, like 'I Palindrome I' by They Might Be Giants). pg: glide (canon, like 'Row Row Row Your Boat'). p4: 4-fold (4/4 time with 4-bar phrases). p6: 6-fold (6/8 time with whole-tone symmetry). p6m: maximal symmetry (only achievable with hexagonal grids, corresponds to the most symmetric possible rhythm). Test: encode 1000 drum patterns as 2D grids, compute their symmetry groups, classify into the 17 wallpaper groups, and compare with musical genre.
directions.title: Crystallographic Groups and Music: The 17 Wallpaper Groups of Rhythm

directions.description: A cellular automaton (CA) rule f: A^Z -> A^Z is a function from configurations to configurations. The CA is reversible if f is bijective. By Hedlund's theorem, a CA is reversible iff its local rule is a permutation. But which CA rules have reversible dynamics? Conjecture: the set of reversible CA rules of radius r on alphabet A is a group under composition, isomorphic to a subgroup of S_{|A|^{2r+1}}. Specifically, the reversibility group G(r, A) is the subgroup of S_{|A|^{2r+1}} generated by the local rules of all reversible CAs of radius r. Conjecture: for binary CAs (A = {0, 1}) with radius r, G(r, {0, 1}) = S_{2^{2r+1}} for r >= 2. This means that any permutation of the 2^{2r+1} possible local neighborhoods can be achieved by composing reversible CA rules. For r = 1 (elementary CAs), G(1, {0, 1}) is a proper subgroup of S_8, and its structure is related to the 256 elementary CA rules. Conjecture: G(1, {0, 1}) has order 8! / 4 = 10080, consisting of the permutations that commute with the shift operator. Test: enumerate all 256 elementary CA rules, identify the reversible ones (Rule 15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240), compute the group generated by their local rules, and verify the structure. Impact: reversible CAs form a group whose structure determines the landscape of reversible computation.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a CA rule f of radius r as f: {0,1}^{2r+1} -> {0,1}. The Wolfram number of f is N = sum_{x=0}^{2^{2r+1}-1} f(x) * 2^x. A CA is reversible iff its global function F: {0,1}^Z -> {0,1}^Z is bijective. Hedlund's theorem: F is bijective iff the local rule is a permutation of neighborhoods that preserves the shift. For r=1: there are 2^8 = 256 rules. The reversible ones are: Rule 15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240 (6 rules). Their local rules as permutations: Rule 170 = left shift (identity on neighborhoods), Rule 15 = NOT(left shift), Rule 51 = complement, Rule 85 = NOT(right shift), Rule 204 = identity (trivial), Rule 240 = right shift. These generate a subgroup of S_8. Conjecture: this subgroup is isomorphic to S_4 (the symmetry group of the square) acting on the 4 non-trivial neighborhoods. For r >= 2: G(r, {0,1}) is conjectured to be S_{2^{2r+1}}, meaning any permutation of neighborhoods is achievable by composing reversible CA rules. Test: compute the group generated by the reversible elementary CA rules using GAP or similar, verify the structure.
directions.title: Galois Theory of Cellular Automata: Which Rules Have Reversible Dynamics?

directions.description: Arrow's impossibility theorem states that no ranked voting system can be fair (Pareto efficient, non-dictatorial, and independent of irrelevant alternatives). The Borsuk-Ulam theorem states that every continuous function f: S^n -> R^n maps some pair of antipodal points to the same value: f(x) = f(-x). Conjecture: Arrow's theorem is a corollary of Borsuk-Ulam. Specifically, define the 'preference sphere' S^{n-1} as the set of all preference profiles over n alternatives, where antipodal points represent opposite preferences (x prefers A > B > C, -x prefers C > B > A). Define f: S^{n-1} -> R^{n-1} by f(x) = (social_preference(x)_1, ..., social_preference(x)_{n-1}). By Borsuk-Ulam, there exists x such that f(x) = f(-x), meaning the social preference for profile x equals the social preference for profile -x. This contradicts Pareto efficiency (if all voters prefer A to B, the social preference should prefer A to B). Therefore, no continuous voting function satisfies all of Arrow's axioms. Conjecture: this proof generalizes: any social choice function on n alternatives is either discontinuous or dictatorial. Test: formalize the Borsuk-Ulam proof of Arrow's theorem in Lean 4. Impact: social choice theory is topology. Arrow's impossibility is a topological theorem about spheres.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the preference sphere: for m voters and n alternatives, a preference profile is (R_1, ..., R_m) where R_i is a strict ranking of n alternatives. The space of all profiles is L(S_n)^m (m copies of the set of linear orders on n elements). Define S^{n-2} as the sphere of 'mood vectors': each point (x_1, ..., x_{n-1}) on S^{n-2} represents a preference intensity, with x_i > 0 meaning alternative i is preferred to alternative n. Antipodal point -x means the reverse preference. Define the social welfare function F: S^{n-2} -> S^{n-2} by F(x) = (w(x)_1, ..., w(x}_{n-1}) where w(x)_i is the social preference for alternative i over n. Arrow's conditions: (1) Pareto: if all voters prefer i to n, then w(x)_i > 0. (2) Non-dictatorship: no single voter determines the outcome. (3) IIA: social preference for i over n depends only on individual preferences for i over n. Borsuk-Ulam: F is continuous (by IIA) and F(-x) = -F(x) (by Pareto). Wait, we need F(x) = F(-x) for some x. Actually: define g(x) = F(x) - F(-x). By Pareto, g is odd: g(-x) = -g(x). By Borsuk-Ulam, g(x) = 0 for some x, giving F(x) = F(-x). But if x represents the preference 'i > n' and -x represents 'n > i', then F(x) = F(-x) means the social preference is indifferent between i and n, contradicting Pareto. Test: formalize in Lean 4.
directions.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem Implies Arrow's Impossibility: Social Choice Is Topology

directions.description: A neural network with ReLU activation defines a piecewise linear function f: R^n -> R^m. The decision boundary of a binary classifier f: R^n -> R is the set {x : f(x) = 0}, which is a piecewise linear hypersurface. The algebraic variety of the decision boundary is the zero set of the polynomial that best approximates f. Conjecture: for a ReLU network with L layers of widths (n, w_1, ..., w_L, 1), the decision boundary is a piecewise linear hypersurface with at most 2^L * prod w_i regions, and the degree of the best polynomial approximation is at most 2^L. More precisely, the decision boundary V(f) = {x : f(x) = 0} is a tropical hypersurface (a piecewise linear object that is the 'skeleton' of an algebraic variety). The tropical variety of the decision boundary has degree at most 2^L and at most prod_{i=1}^{L} (w_i choose 2) singularities. Conjecture: the VC dimension of a ReLU network with L layers and total width W is at most L * W * log(W), matching the known bound up to log factors. Test: train ReLU networks on synthetic data, extract decision boundaries, and verify they are tropical hypersurfaces with the predicted degree and singularity count. Impact: neural network decision boundaries are tropical varieties. The complexity of the network (L, W) determines the algebraic complexity of the boundary.
directions.proof_strategy: A ReLU network f: R^n -> R with L layers computes a piecewise linear function. The number of linear regions is at most prod_{i=1}^{L} sum_{j=0}^{min(n,w_i)} (w_i choose j) (Montufar et al., 2014). For wide networks (w_i >= n): this is at most prod_{i=1}^{L} 2^{w_i-1} = 2^{sum w_i - L}. The decision boundary B = {x : f(x) = 0} is a piecewise linear hypersurface. Each linear piece of f defines a halfspace, and B is the union of boundaries of these halfspaces. The algebraic approximation: by the Weierstrass approximation theorem, there exists a polynomial p of degree d such that ||f - p|| < epsilon. The variety V(p) = {x : p(x) = 0} approximates B. For piecewise linear f with K regions, the degree of p needed is d ~ K^{1/n} (by approximation theory). The tropical variety: V(f) is a tropical hypersurface defined by the tropical polynomial max_j(alpha_j + x . beta_j) where the max is over the linear pieces. The degree of this tropical polynomial is the number of different linear pieces, which is at most 2^L. The singularities of V(f) are points where 3+ linear pieces meet, and there are at most prod (w_i choose 2) such points. Test: train 2-layer and 3-layer ReLU networks on 2D synthetic data, extract the decision boundary, count linear regions and singularities, verify against the bounds.
directions.title: Algebraic Geometry of Neural Networks: Varieties of Decision Boundaries

directions.description: The Collatz conjecture (3n+1 problem) states that every positive integer eventually reaches 1 under the map T(n) = n/2 (n even) or 3n+1 (n odd). Despite being verified up to 2^68, a proof remains elusive. Conjecture: the Collatz conjecture is independent of Peano Arithmetic (PA). That is, PA can neither prove nor refute the statement 'for all n, the Collatz sequence starting at n eventually reaches 1'. This would mean the conjecture is TRUE (in the standard model) but UNPROVABLE in PA. The argument: the Collatz map is a Diophantine function that grows faster than any provably total computable function in PA. Specifically, the halting problem for Collatz (does the orbit of n reach 1?) is at least as hard as the consistency of PA, which by Godel's second incompleteness theorem is unprovable in PA. Conjecture: the Collatz conjecture is equivalent to Con(PA) over a weak base theory, meaning that if PA is consistent, then PA does not prove Collatz. Test: formalize the equivalence between Collatz and Con(PA) in Lean 4. Show that a counterexample to Collatz (an n whose orbit diverges or cycles) would imply not-Con(PA). Impact: Collatz might be the simplest true-but-unprovable statement in arithmetic — a concrete example of Godel's incompleteness.
directions.proof_strategy: The argument proceeds in three steps. Step 1: Show that the Collatz halting problem (given n, does T^k(n) = 1 for some k?) is Pi^0_2-complete. This means it is at least as hard as any Pi^0_2 statement, including Con(PA). Step 2: Show that if Collatz is false (there exists n whose orbit diverges or cycles), then Con(PA) implies a contradiction. This would mean not-Collatz implies not-Con(PA), i.e., Collatz follows from Con(PA). Step 3: Show that if Collatz is true, then PA cannot prove it, because the proof would require a consistency-strength beyond PA. The key: the Collatz map can simulate any Turing machine. Specifically, Conway (1972) showed that a generalization of the Collatz map (the 'Fractran' language) is Turing-complete. The specific 3n+1 map is not known to be Turing-complete, but it is conjectured that the set of Collatz orbits encodes the set of PA-proofs. If this is the case, then Collatz is equivalent to Con(PA). Test: formalize the Fractran encoding of Turing machines in Lean 4, show that the 3n+1 map can simulate a register machine, and establish the reduction from Collatz to Con(PA).
directions.title: The Collatz Conjecture Is Undecidable: What If 3n+1 Can't Be Proved?

directions.description: The Alexander polynomial Delta_K(t) of a knot K is a Laurent polynomial that encodes topological information about the knot. Conjecture: for any knot K with n crossings, the Alexander polynomial Delta_K(t) can be expressed as the generating function of lattice paths in Z^2 that avoid a region determined by the knot diagram. Specifically, define the 'knot lattice' L_K as the set of lattice paths from (0,0) to (n,n) that avoid the 'forbidden region' R_K determined by the crossing structure of K. Then Delta_K(t) = sum_{p in L_K} t^{area(p)} where area(p) is the area under the path p. This conjecture follows from the state sum formula for the Alexander polynomial: Delta_K(t) = sum_{states s} (-1)^{w(s)} t^{a(s)} where w(s) is the writhe and a(s) is the area of the state. The area a(s) is exactly the area under a lattice path determined by the state. Conjecture: every Alexander polynomial arises as a lattice path generating function, and vice versa. This means the Alexander polynomial is not just a knot invariant — it is a combinatorial object that counts lattice paths. Test: compute the Alexander polynomials for the first 50 knots and verify that each can be expressed as a lattice path generating function. Impact: knot invariants are combinatorial. The Alexander polynomial counts lattice paths, connecting topology to combinatorics.
directions.proof_strategy: The Alexander polynomial Delta_K(t) is computed from the Alexander module H_1(X_K, Z[t, t^{-1}]) where X_K is the infinite cyclic cover of the knot complement. The presentation matrix (Alexander matrix) has entries that are Laurent polynomials. Delta_K(t) = det(M) where M is the (n-1) x (n-1) Alexander matrix after deleting one row and one column. Lattice path connection: the state sum for Delta_K(t) can be written as Delta_K(t) = sum_{s in states} t^{area(s)} * (-1)^{writhe(s)}. Each state s corresponds to a lattice path from (0,0) to (n,n) in Z^2, and area(s) is the area under this path. The forbidden region R_K is determined by the over/under crossings: at each crossing, the path must go either above or below the crossing, and the forbidden region is the set of paths that violate the knot's crossing constraints. More precisely: for a knot diagram with n crossings, each crossing is resolved as either A-type (horizontal pass) or B-type (vertical pass). The lattice path goes from (0,0) to (2,n) stepping right (A-type) or up (B-type) at each crossing. The area under the path is the sum of the vertical positions. Delta_K(t) = sum_{paths avoiding R_K} t^{area(path)}. Test: for the trefoil (3_1), compute the 8 lattice paths from (0,0) to (2,3), identify the 2 paths that avoid the forbidden region, and verify that the sum of t^{area} matches the Alexander polynomial Delta_{3_1}(t) = t - 1 + t^{-1}.

directions.description: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has non-trivial zeros at s = 1/2 + i*gamma_n on the critical line (assuming RH). These zeros encode deep arithmetic information. Conjecture: the zeros gamma_n are the spectrum of a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space, and this operator is the Casimir element of a quantum group G_q. Specifically, define the 'zeta quantum group' G_q as the q-deformation of SU(2) where q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} (using the first zero gamma_1 ~ 14.13). The Casimir element C_q of G_q has eigenvalues that are quadratic functions of the representation labels, and the spectrum of C_q is {n(n+1) : n in N}. Conjecture: the Riemann zeros gamma_n are related to the spectrum of C_q by gamma_n = f(spectrum(C_q)) for some function f. If f is linear, this would mean the zeros are evenly spaced, which is false (the zeros have Poisson-like spacings). If f is logarithmic, gamma_n ~ pi*n/log(n) which matches the average spacing. Conjecture: the spectral statistics of C_q match the GUE random matrix statistics of the Riemann zeros (Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture). Test: compute the spectrum of C_q for G_q with q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} and compare the spectral statistics with the Riemann zeros. Impact: the Riemann hypothesis is a representation-theoretic statement about quantum groups.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the quantum group SU_q(2) with q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} where gamma_1 ~ 14.13 is the first Riemann zero. The representation theory: irreducible representations V_n of dimension n+1 for n = 0, 1, 2, .... The Casimir element C_q acts on V_n with eigenvalue [n]_q * [n+1]_q where [m]_q = (q^m - q^{-m})/(q - q^{-1}) is the q-integer. For q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1}: [m]_q = sin(m * pi * gamma_1) / sin(pi * gamma_1). The eigenvalues of C_q on V_n are: lambda_n = [n]_q * [n+1]_q = sin(n*pi*gamma_1) * sin((n+1)*pi*gamma_1) / sin(pi*gamma_1)^2. Conjecture: the set {lambda_n : n >= 1} encodes the Riemann zeros in a way that preserves their statistical properties. Specifically, the level spacings {lambda_{n+1} - lambda_n} should follow the GUE distribution (Wigner-Dyson surmise). Test: compute lambda_n for n = 1..1000, compute the level spacings, and compare with the GUE distribution P(s) = (32/pi^2) * s^2 * exp(-4*s^2/pi^2). Also compare with the Riemann zero spacings. This requires numerical computation of q-deformed representations.
directions.title: Quantum Groups from Number Theory: The Riemann Hypothesis as a Representation Problem

directions.description:
# Future Directions — The Topology of Arithmetic

This cycle established that the zero-dimensional persistent homology of the prime
point cloud is a genuine persistence module whose entire structure — functorial
merging, total persistence, global merge scale, unbounded bars, and Betti number —
is read off the sequence of prime gaps. The following conjectures push that
correspondence further.

## 1. The barcode length distribution follows the Hardy–Littlewood law

**Conjecture.** For each even `g`, the asymptotic density of H₀ bars of death scale
exactly `g` among the first `N` bars is proportional to the Hardy–Littlewood
singular series for gap `g`; in particular bars of length `2`, `4`, and `6` occur
with the classically predicted relative frequencies, and no even length is ever
absent from arbitrarily long windows.

*The key insight is* that a bar of death scale `g` is exactly a maximal run whose
bounding gap equals `g`, so the bar-length histogram of the barcode is literally
the prime-gap histogram, transporting the entire analytic theory of gap
distribution into a topological invariant.

*Why now?* The present cycle proved the barcode is unbounded and that its bar
lengths are precisely the gaps; the natural next quantitative step is the
distribution of those lengths, for which the Hardy–Littlewood conjectures give a
sharp, testable target.

## 2. Total persistence grows like `n log n`

**Conjecture.** The total persistence of the first `n` bars — proved here to equal
`p_n − 2` — satisfies `p_n − 2 ∼ n log n`, and more precisely the normalized total
persistence `(p_n − 2)/(n log n) → 1`.

*The key insight is* that total persistence is not an independent analytic quantity
but is identically the `n`-th prime minus two, so the growth rate of aggregate
topological persistence is exactly the prime number theorem in disguise.

*Why now?* With the telescoping identity `total_persistence = p_n − 2` in hand, the
asymptotics of total persistence reduce to a known and provable statement about
`p_n`, making this the most immediately reachable refinement.

## 3. The Betti curve has a universal staircase profile

**Conjecture.** Viewed as a function of the scale `ε`, the Betti number
`b₀(ε, n) = 1 + #{gaps ≤ n exceeding ε}` is a right-continuous decreasing step
function whose rescaled profile, under `ε ↦ ε / log p_n`, converges to a
deterministic limiting curve as `n → ∞`.

*The key insight is* that each downward step of the Betti curve is triggered by one
prime gap crossing the threshold `ε`, so the shape of the curve is a cumulative
count of gaps and its limiting profile encodes the limiting law of normalized
prime gaps.

*Why now?* This cycle gave the exact finite-scale formula for `b₀`; converting an
exact counting formula into a scaling limit is the standard and now well-motivated
continuation.

## 4. Higher-dimensional prime clouds carry genuine loops

**Conjecture.** Placing the primes on a curve in the plane by `p_n ↦ (p_n, p_{n+1})`
(consecutive-pair embedding) yields a point cloud whose first persistent homology
`H₁` is non-trivial: there exist persistent one-dimensional cycles whose birth and
death scales are controlled by consecutive triples of gaps.

*The key insight is* that correlations between neighbouring gaps — invisible to the
one-dimensional cloud, whose `H₁` vanishes — become geometric loops once the primes
are lifted to a gap-recording curve, turning gap correlations into topology.

*Why now?* The one-dimensional theory is now complete and shows `H₁` is trivial on
the line; the first place new topology can appear is the two-dimensional lift,
which is the minimal setting where gap correlations can close up into cycles.

## 5. The merge tree of the primes is a self-similar random-like tree

**Conjecture.** The single-linkage merge tree of the prime cloud — whose internal
node heights are the successive record gaps — is, after normalization, statistically
indistinguishable from the merge tree of a Poisson process with slowly varying
intensity `1/log x`, in the sense of convergence of its scaled height profile.

*The key insight is* that single-linkage clustering on a line is entirely determined
by the gaps, so the merge tree of the primes is a deterministic functional of the
gap sequence, and its comparison to a Poisson model is a precise formulation of the
heuristic that primes behave like random numbers with density `1/log x`.

*Why now?* Having identified components with fibres of the component-root map and
the merge scale with the maximum gap, the merge tree is now a fully specified
combinatorial object ready for a distributional comparison.

directions.description: Ramsey's theorem states that any 2-coloring of the edges of K_6 contains a monochromatic K_3 (a triangle of one color). Applied to DNA: any sequence of 4^6 + 1 = 4097 nucleotides must contain a repeated 6-mer (by pigeonhole). But Ramsey theory for subsequences is more subtle: what is the minimum length L(k) of a DNA sequence over {A, C, G, T} such that every subsequence of length k contains a repeated 4-mer? Conjecture: L(k) = Theta(k * 4^4 * log(4^4)) = Theta(k * 256 * 8) = Theta(k * 2048). More precisely, by the Lovasz local lemma, L(k) >= 4^{4k/5} for sequences that avoid repeated k-mers in all subsequences. Conjecture: for real genomes, the actual L(k) is much smaller because real DNA has low complexity regions (microsatellites, Alu repeats) that create forced repeats. Specifically, the human genome has L(4) ~ 1000 (any 1000 consecutive bases contain a repeated 4-mer in some subsequence), while the random genome has L(4) ~ 4^4 * log(4^4) ~ 5000. Test: compute L(k) for real genomes vs random genomes and verify the factor-of-5 compression. Impact: DNA avoids subsequential repeats in a way that Ramsey theory predicts, but real genomes are 5x more 'forced' than random sequences.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the subsequence Ramsey number L(k, s, alphabet) as the minimum length of a sequence over the given alphabet such that every subsequence of length k contains a repeated s-mer. For DNA: alphabet = {A, C, G, T}, s = 4 (4-mers). L(k, 4, 4) = minimum length of a DNA sequence such that every length-k subsequence has a repeated 4-mer. By the pigeonhole principle: any sequence of length 4^4 + 1 = 257 has a repeated 4-mer (not subsequence, but substring). For subsequences: we need every length-k subsequence to contain a repeated 4-mer. The longest sequence with NO subsequence of length k containing a repeated 4-mer is called the 'subsequence-Ramsey avoidance sequence'. Conjecture: this sequence has length O(k * 4^4 * log(4^4)). Proof sketch: by the Lovasz local lemma, the probability that a random sequence of length n avoids repeated 4-mers in all subsequences is positive when n < k * 4^4 * log(4^4). Test: generate random DNA sequences of varying lengths, extract all subsequences of length k, check for repeated 4-mers. Compare with real genomes (human chromosome 1, E. coli genome). Verify that real genomes hit the threshold at L ~ 1000 (much shorter than the random L ~ 5000).
directions.title: The Ramsey Theory of DNA: Subsequence Avoidance in Genetic Codes

directions.description: Entropy H(X) = -sum p(x) log p(x) measures the information content of a random variable. In category theory, a functor F: C -> D 'loses information' when it maps non-isomorphic objects to isomorphic ones. Define the 'functorial entropy' H(F) as the expected information lost by F: H(F) = -sum_{d in Ob(D)} p(d) * log(p(d)) where p(d) = |F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|. Conjecture: For the forgetful functor U: Top -> Set that forgets the topology, H(U) = log(2^{aleph_0}) = aleph_0 (infinite entropy, because uncountably many topologies map to the same set). For the abelianization functor Ab: Grp -> AbGrp, H(Ab) = log(2) (each abelian group has 2 non-abelian preimages on average: G and G x Z/2Z). For the inclusion functor Inc: FinGrp -> Grp, H(Inc) = 0 (no information loss, since finite groups embed as themselves). Conjecture: H(F) = 0 iff F is faithful, and H(F) = infinity iff F identifies infinitely many non-isomorphic objects. For finite categories: H(F) = log(|Ob(C)| / |Ob(D)|) when F is 'uniform' (each fiber has the same size). Test: compute H(F) for various functors between finite categories and verify the formula. Impact: entropy is not just a measure-theoretic concept — it is the information-theoretic shadow of functoriality. Every functor loses information, and the entropy measures how much.
directions.proof_strategy: Define functorial entropy: for a functor F: C -> D between finite categories, H(F) = -sum_{d in Ob(D)} (|F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|) * log(|F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|). This measures the information lost when F identifies non-isomorphic objects. Properties: (1) H(F) >= 0, with equality iff F is injective on objects up to isomorphism (i.e., F maps non-isomorphic objects to non-isomorphic objects). (2) H(F) is maximized when all fibers have the same size: H(F) = log(|Ob(C)| / |Ob(D)|). (3) H(G circ F) >= H(F) + H(G) for composable functors (subadditivity). (4) For the forgetful functor U: Top -> Set: H(U) = infinity because |F^{-1}(S)| = infinity for every set S with |S| >= 2 (there are uncountably many topologies on S). (5) For abelianization Ab: Grp -> AbGrp: each abelian group A has |F^{-1}(A)| = infinity (there are infinitely many non-abelian groups with abelianization A), so H(Ab) = infinity. Wait, this contradicts the conjecture. Correction: for finite groups, Ab: FinGrp -> FinAbGrp. Each finite abelian group A has finitely many preimages. H(Ab) = log(sum |F^{-1}(A)| / |FinAbGrp|). For small groups: Z/2Z has preimages Z/2Z (abelian) and S_3 (non-abelian with abelianization Z/2Z). Z/3Z has preimages Z/3Z and... (need to enumerate). Test: enumerate all groups of order <= 32, compute their abelianizations, and calculate H(Ab).
directions.title: Categorification of Entropy: The Information Loss of Functors

directions.description: The Hodge conjecture states that every rational cohomology class on a projective variety is a rational linear combination of algebraic cycles. For a ReLU neural network f: R^n -> R, the decision surface V(f) = {x : f(x) = 0} is a piecewise linear hypersurface. Conjecture: every rational homology class in H_{n-2}(V(f), Q) is represented by an algebraic cycle (a subvariety of V(f) of codimension 1). Since V(f) is piecewise linear, its homology groups are finitely generated and every cycle is a formal sum of linear pieces. Each linear piece is an algebraic cycle (a hyperplane section). Conjecture: the piecewise linear Hodge conjecture holds — every homology class in V(f) is a sum of hyperplane sections. This is TRUE for piecewise linear varieties because every face of a polyhedron is cut out by a linear equation. The deeper conjecture: for a ReLU network with L layers and widths (n, w_1, ..., w_L, 1), the Hodge numbers h^{p,q}(V(f)) satisfy h^{p,q} <= (w_1 choose p) * (w_L choose q) * prod_{i=2}^{L-1} w_i. Test: compute H_{n-2}(V(f)) for small ReLU networks and verify that every class is represented by hyperplane sections. Impact: the Hodge conjecture is trivially true for neural network decision surfaces. The non-trivial content is the BOUND on Hodge numbers.
directions.proof_strategy: For a ReLU network f: R^n -> R with L layers, the decision surface V(f) is a polyhedral complex. Each linear region of f defines a halfspace H_i = {x : a_i . x + b_i > 0}, and V(f) is the union of boundaries of these halfspaces. The homology H_{n-2}(V(f), Z) is generated by the (n-2)-dimensional faces of V(f). Each such face is the intersection of exactly 2 hyperplanes: face_{ij} = {x : a_i . x + b_i = 0, a_j . x + b_j = 0}. Each face is an algebraic cycle (a codimension-2 subvariety of R^n cut out by 2 linear equations). The Hodge conjecture for V(f): every class in H_{n-2}(V(f), Q) is represented by a formal sum of these faces. This is trivially true because H_{n-2}(V(f), Z) is free abelian generated by the faces. The non-trivial content: the NUMBER of faces is bounded by (w_1 choose 2) * prod_{i=2}^{L} w_i (the product of binomial coefficients of widths). This gives the Hodge number bound h^{1,1}(V(f)) <= (w_1 choose 2) * prod w_i. More generally, h^{p,q}(V(f)) <= (w_1 choose p) * (w_L choose q) * prod w_i. Test: for a 2-layer ReLU network with n=2, w_1=4, compute V(f), enumerate faces, compute H_0(V(f)), and verify every class is a sum of vertices.
directions.title: The Hodge Conjecture for Neural Networks: Algebraic Cycles in Decision Surfaces

directions.description: An automatic sequence is one generated by a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). The Thue-Morse sequence 01101001... is 2-automatic. The Rudin-Shapiro sequence is 2-automatic. The paperfolding sequence is 2-automatic. Conjecture: a sequence (a_n) is k-automatic iff its generating function G(x) = sum a_n x^n is algebraic over Q(x) of degree at most k. This is known (Christol's theorem): a formal power series over F_k is algebraic iff its coefficient sequence is k-automatic. But Christol's theorem only works over finite fields. For sequences over Z (or Q), the conjecture is: a sequence (a_n) over Z is k-automatic iff it satisfies a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients of degree at most k-1 in n. Conjecture: the halting problem for k-automatic sequences is decidable: given a DFA that generates (a_n), it is decidable whether there exists n such that a_n = 0 (the 'zero in sequence' problem). This is TRUE for k-automatic sequences (by the pumping lemma: if the DFA accepts any string, it accepts an infinite number, so a_n = 0 infinitely often). But for morphic sequences (generalizations of automatic sequences), the problem is open. Conjecture: the zero-in-sequence problem for morphic sequences is decidable. Test: implement the decidability algorithm for k-automatic sequences and verify on 100 test sequences. Impact: automatic sequences have decidable halting problems. The boundary between decidability and undecidability in sequence theory is the boundary between automatic and morphic.
directions.proof_strategy: Christol's theorem: a formal power series f(x) = sum a_n x^n over F_p is algebraic (satisfies a polynomial equation P(x, f(x)) = 0 with P in F_p[x,y]) iff the sequence (a_n) is p-automatic (generated by a DFA with p input symbols). The DFA reads n in base p and outputs a_n. For sequences over Z: a sequence (a_n) is k-automatic iff it is the image under a coding of a fixed point of a k-uniform morphism. The zero-in-sequence problem: given a k-automatic sequence (a_n), decide if there exists n such that a_n = 0. Algorithm: build the DFA M for (a_n). The sequence has a zero iff M accepts any string (i.e., there is a path from the start state to an accepting state). This is simply a reachability problem in the DFA, which is decidable in O(|M|) time by BFS/DFS. The key insight: automatic sequences are ultimately periodic (by the pumping lemma), so if a_n = 0 for some n, then a_n = 0 for infinitely many n. For morphic sequences: the problem is open. A morphic sequence is the image under a coding of a fixed point of a non-uniform morphism. The zero-in-sequence problem for morphic sequences is equivalent to deciding whether the fixed point of a morphism contains a given symbol. This is known to be decidable for primitive morphisms (by the Perron-Frobenius theorem) but open in general. Test: implement the reachability algorithm for k-automatic sequences, verify on Thue-Morse (has zeros), the constant-1 sequence (no zeros), and 100 random automatic sequences.
directions.title: Automatic Sequences and the Halting Problem: When Is a Sequence Computable?

directions.description: An argumentation framework AF = (A, R) consists of a set of arguments A and an attack relation R subset A x A. The preferred extensions of AF are the maximal admissible sets (subsets S of A that defend themselves against all attacks and are maximal with this property). Conjecture: the preferred extensions of AF form a simplicial complex K(AF) on the vertex set A. The homology groups H_n(K(AF)) measure the 'holes' in the argumentation structure. H_0 measures the number of connected components (independent debate threads). H_1 measures circular arguments (cycles where each argument attacks the next, and the last attacks the first). H_2 measures 'spheres' of arguments (3D cycles where arguments form a spherical shell). Conjecture: for any argumentation framework, the Euler characteristic chi(K(AF)) = |A| - |R| + sum_{n>=2} (-1)^n * dim(H_n) equals |preferred extensions| - |grounded extension size|. This connects the topology of the argument to its semantics. Test: construct K(AF) for 100 argumentation frameworks from debate transcripts, compute homology groups, and verify the Euler characteristic formula. Impact: arguments have topology. Circular arguments are 1-holes, and 3D argument spheres are 2-holes. The shape of a debate is a topological invariant.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the argumentation complex K(AF): vertices = arguments in A, simplices = independent sets (subsets S of A such that no two arguments in S attack each other). The independent sets form a simplicial complex because if S is independent, so is any subset of S. This is the 'clique complex' of the complement of the attack graph. Properties: (1) preferred extensions are maximal simplices of K(AF). (2) stable extensions are maximal simplices that are also 'dominating' (every argument not in S is attacked by some argument in S). (3) The grounded extension is the intersection of all preferred extensions, which is the 'core' of K(AF). The homology H_n(K(AF)) measures: H_0 = number of connected debate threads (components of the complement of R). H_1 = circular arguments (cycles in the attack graph where a1 attacks a2, a2 attacks a3, ..., a_k attacks a1). H_2 = 3D argument spheres (sets of arguments that form a spherical shell of attacks). The Euler characteristic: chi(K(AF)) = sum_{n>=0} (-1)^n * dim(H_n) = sum_{n>=0} (-1)^n * f_n where f_n is the number of n-simplices. Conjecture: chi(K(AF)) = |preferred extensions| - |grounded extension|. Test: construct AFs from debate data, compute K(AF), calculate homology and Euler characteristic, verify the formula.
directions.title: The Topology of Argumentation: Why Debates Have Holes

directions.description: The natural gradient algorithm updates parameters theta in the direction of steepest descent on the Fisher information manifold: theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta * G^{-1}(theta_t) * gradient L(theta_t) where G is the Fisher information matrix. This is equivalent to following the geodesic on the statistical manifold (the Riemannian manifold with metric G). Conjecture: for any optimization problem with loss function L, the natural gradient descent converges to the minimum in O(1/t) iterations, regardless of the condition number of G. This is because the natural gradient follows the geodesic, which is the shortest path on the manifold, and the path length is O(1) (bounded by the diameter of the manifold). In contrast, standard gradient descent takes O(kappa) iterations where kappa is the condition number of G. Conjecture: natural gradient descent with step size eta = 1/t achieves L(theta_t) - L(theta*) = O(1/t) for convex losses, and L(theta_t) - L(theta*) = O(exp(-t/d)) for strongly convex losses, where d is the dimension. Test: compare natural gradient descent and standard gradient descent on logistic regression with varying condition numbers, verify the convergence rates. Impact: optimization is geometry. The natural gradient is the geodesic on the Fisher manifold, and geodesics are the shortest paths.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the statistical manifold M = {p(x|theta) : theta in R^d} with the Fisher metric G(theta) = E_{p(x|theta)}[nabla_theta log p(x|theta) nabla_theta log p(x|theta)^T]. The natural gradient is: tilde{nabla} L = G^{-1}(theta) * nabla_theta L. Natural gradient descent: theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta_t * tilde{nabla} L(theta_t). Convergence analysis: for convex L, the natural gradient descent is equivalent to mirror descent with the Bregman divergence generated by the log-partition function. The convergence rate for mirror descent is O(1/t) for convex objectives and O(exp(-t/d)) for strongly convex objectives. Key insight: the natural gradient reparametrizes the problem so that the Fisher metric becomes the identity, 'whitening' the landscape. This is equivalent to following the geodesic on M, which is the shortest path from theta_0 to theta*. The geodesic distance d(theta_0, theta*) = O(sqrt(d)) (bounded by the diameter of the parameter space). Natural gradient descent covers this distance in O(d) steps, giving convergence rate O(exp(-1/d)). Test: implement natural gradient descent for logistic regression (where G(theta) = X^T diag(p(1-p)) X), compare with standard GD for condition numbers kappa = 1, 10, 100, 1000. Measure convergence rate L(theta_t) - L(theta*) vs t.
directions.title: Information Geometry of Optimization: Natural Gradient Follows Geodesics

directions.description: A Sudoku puzzle is a constraint satisfaction problem on a 9x9 grid. The 'spectral gap' of a Sudoku puzzle is the gap between the two largest eigenvalues of the transition matrix of the Markov chain that randomly swaps two compatible entries. The spectral gap determines the mixing time: the number of swaps needed to generate a uniformly random solution. Conjecture: the spectral gap of a Sudoku puzzle undergoes a phase transition at the critical density d_c = 17/81 (the density of the minimal number of clues, 17, divided by 81). For puzzles with fewer than 17 clues, the spectral gap is large (the Markov chain mixes quickly, meaning there are many solutions). For puzzles with exactly 17 clues, the spectral gap is minimal (the chain mixes slowly, meaning solutions are hard to find). For puzzles with more than 30 clues, the spectral gap is zero (the chain is reducible, meaning the puzzle has a unique solution and no swaps are possible). Conjecture: the spectral gap lambda_1 - lambda_2 of the Sudoku Markov chain satisfies: lambda_1 - lambda_2 > epsilon for d < 17/81 (many solutions, fast mixing), lambda_1 - lambda_2 ~ 0 for d ~ 17/81 (critical point, slow mixing), and the chain is absorbing for d > 30/81 (unique solution, no mixing). Test: compute the spectral gap for Sudoku puzzles with varying numbers of clues and verify the phase transition. Impact: Sudoku has a spectral gap phase transition. The hardness of the puzzle is determined by the gap, not by the number of clues.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Sudoku Markov chain M: state space = valid completions of the puzzle. Transitions: swap two compatible entries (entries in different rows, columns, and boxes). The transition matrix P has entries P(i,j) = probability of moving from state i to state j. The spectral gap is lambda_1 - lambda_2 where lambda_1 = 1 (the stationary distribution eigenvalue) and lambda_2 is the second-largest eigenvalue. For a connected state space (many solutions): lambda_1 - lambda_2 > 0, and the mixing time is O(1/(lambda_1 - lambda_2)). For a unique solution: the chain has only one state, so lambda_1 = lambda_2 = 1 (no gap). For critical puzzles (17 clues): the state space has many solutions but they are 'far apart' (connected only through long chains of swaps), so lambda_2 is close to 1 and the gap is small. Phase transition conjecture: as the number of clues k increases from 0 to 81, the spectral gap lambda_1 - lambda_2 transitions from large (many solutions, fast mixing) to small (few solutions, slow mixing) to zero (unique solution, no mixing). The critical point is k = 17 (the minimum number of clues for a unique solution). Test: generate Sudoku puzzles with k = 17, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 clues, compute the transition matrix M for the swap Markov chain, find eigenvalues, measure spectral gap. For k >= 30 (unique solution), the chain has 1 state.
directions.title: The Spectral Gap of Sudoku: When Puzzles Become Phase Transitions

directions.description: A ReLU network f: R -> R with L layers of width w is a piecewise linear function with at most w^L pieces. By the universal approximation theorem, such networks can approximate any continuous function. But HOW WELL can they approximate specific constants? Conjecture: a ReLU network with L layers of width w can approximate pi to within epsilon using O(w * L * log(1/epsilon)) parameters. More precisely, there exists a ReLU network f with L = O(log(log(1/epsilon))) layers and w = O(log(1/epsilon)) width such that |f(1) - pi| < epsilon. This is because pi can be computed by the Leibniz formula pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ..., and a ReLU network can implement the partial sums. The number of terms needed is O(1/epsilon), and each term can be computed by a constant-depth ReLU subnetwork. The depth needed is O(log(1/epsilon)) for the sum and O(log(log(1/epsilon))) for the individual terms. Conjecture: the approximation rate for rational numbers by ReLU networks is O(1/(w^L)), matching the piecewise linear structure. For irrational numbers like pi, the rate is O(1/(w * L * 2^L)), which is slower but still exponential in depth. Test: construct ReLU networks that approximate pi, e, and sqrt(2) and measure the approximation error as a function of network size. Impact: ReLU networks approximate constants at a rate determined by their depth and width. Pi requires O(log(log(1/epsilon))) depth.
directions.proof_strategy: Leibniz formula: pi/4 = sum_{k=0}^{infinity} (-1)^k / (2k+1). The partial sum S_n = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^k / (2k+1) approximates pi/4 with error O(1/n). To achieve |f(1) - pi| < epsilon, we need n = O(1/epsilon) terms. ReLU implementation: each term t_k = (-1)^k / (2k+1) can be computed as t_k = ReLU(1/(2k+1)) - 2*ReLU(1/(2k+1) - 1/2) (alternating sign). The division 1/(2k+1) requires a ReLU network with O(log(k)) depth (using binary long division). The sum of n terms requires O(log(n)) depth (tree reduction). Total: L = O(log(n) + log(log(n))) = O(log(1/epsilon)) layers. Width: w = O(n) for parallel summation, or w = O(1) for sequential summation with O(n) depth. For the tree reduction: L = O(log(1/epsilon)), w = O(1/epsilon). Better construction: use Machin's formula pi/4 = 4*arctan(1/5) - arctan(1/239), which converges much faster. arctan(1/n) = 1/n - 1/(3n^3) + 1/(5n^5) - ... converges in O(n) terms. For Machin: n terms give error O(1/5^{2n+1}), so only O(log(1/epsilon)) terms needed. Total: L = O(log(log(1/epsilon))), w = O(log(1/epsilon)). Test: implement in Python + Lean 4, measure approximation error vs network size.
directions.title: Diophantine Approximation on Neural Networks: How Well Can ReLU Approximate Pi?

directions.description:
# Future Directions: Geometry of the Logistic–Tent Conjugacy

This cycle established an exact topological conjugacy between the smooth logistic
map `f(x)=4x(1-x)` and the piecewise-linear tent map `T(t)=1-|2t-1|`, implemented
by the strictly increasing homeomorphism `h(t)=sin²(πt/2)` of the unit interval.
Fixed points, a period-two orbit, and the intertwining of all iterates transfer
verbatim between the two systems. The following conjectures push the same
geometric bridge further.

## 1. Every period is realised, and the count is exponential

**Conjecture.** For each `n ≥ 1` the logistic map has exactly `2ⁿ` points of period
dividing `n` in the unit interval, and it possesses points of *exact* period `n`
for every `n`.

The key insight is that the conjugacy reduces counting logistic periodic points to
counting tent periodic points, and the tent map's `n`-fold iterate is a sawtooth
with `2ⁿ` full ramps, each crossing the diagonal exactly once. Why now? The exact
conjugacy `fⁿ = h ∘ Tⁿ ∘ h⁻¹` and the bijectivity of `h` are already in hand, so
the transcendental fixed-point count for `f` becomes a purely combinatorial count
of sawtooth crossings.

## 2. Density of periodic seeds and topological transitivity

**Conjecture.** The periodic points of the logistic map are dense in `[0,1]`, and
the map is topologically transitive; together with sensitive dependence this
certifies Devaney chaos on the whole interval.

The key insight is that a homeomorphism preserves density and transitivity, so it
suffices to prove them for the tent map, where periodic seeds are the dyadic-type
rationals `k/(2ⁿ±1)` and are manifestly dense. Why now? With `h` proven to be a
homeomorphism, every topological property of the tent map — the transparent model
— transfers directly to the logistic map without any smooth analysis.

## 3. Invariant density and the arcsine law

**Conjecture.** The logistic map preserves the arcsine measure with density
`1 / (π √(x(1-x)))`, which is exactly the pushforward under `h` of the uniform
(Lebesgue) measure preserved by the tent map.

The key insight is that `h` conjugates the uniform-preserving tent map to the
logistic map, so the invariant density of `f` must be the image of the flat density
under the change of variables `x = sin²(πt/2)`, whose Jacobian produces the arcsine
weight. Why now? The explicit, differentiable conjugating map `h` makes the
change-of-variables computation elementary, turning a statement about a smooth
chaotic system into a one-line pushforward of Lebesgue measure.

## 4. Cryptographic fragility is coordinate-independent

**Conjecture.** Any invariant an attacker can compute from a logistic keystream
(bias, autocorrelation, algebraic degree of seed recovery) has an exact tent-map
counterpart obtainable by applying `h⁻¹`; hence the "chaos cipher" offers no
security beyond its piecewise-linear shadow.

The key insight is that a keystream masked by logistic iterates is, in the `h`
coordinate, masked by tent iterates — a binary shift map whose bits are read
directly off the seed. Why now? The exact conjugacy makes "look how complicated
the parabola orbit is" quantifiable: complexity claimed in the smooth coordinate
evaporates in the conjugate linear coordinate, giving a rigorous no-go statement
for logistic-map stream ciphers.
